title: Wyckoff Spring
teaches: The Wyckoff spring as we teach it: in a leader above its 200-day, resting in a flat sideways range, price dips a little under the floor and closes back inside. We read the range, the depth of the dip (0.1 to 1 ATR) and the close, buy the reclaim or the later quiet test, put the stop a few cents under the spring low, and take the stop as the trade, because a spring that fails usually fails at once. A single swing low is a 2B, a rising average is an undercut and rally, and a dip of 2 ATR or more is a breakdown.

questions.q: In the Wyckoff school, what is a spring?
choices: A quick dip under support, then back
A breakout over resistance that holds
A drop that closes below support
questions.answer: A quick dip under support, then back
questions.why: A quick dip under support, then back in. Pruden defines a spring as a move below the support of a trading range that quickly reverses back into the range. ChartSchool adds that it closes back within the range. Speed matters: Taylor calls slower violations that fail washouts or bear traps, not springs.
questions.lesson_line: A spring dips under the floor and snaps back inside.

wrong.A breakout over resistance that holds: That is a breakout. A spring goes under support, not over resistance.
wrong.A slow slide through support: A spring reverses quickly. Slower violations that fail are washouts or bear traps.
wrong.A drop that closes below support: That is a breakdown. A spring reverses to close back within the range.

questions.q: Where in the range does a spring usually occur?
choices: On the first day of the range
At any point; timing is random
questions.why: Late in the range. ChartSchool says springs or shakeouts usually occur late within a range, and Fraser says the spring typically develops later in the accumulation. Pruden, a separate publisher, agrees: the late spring lets the market make a definitive test of the supply left. It is a tendency, not a fixed day count.
questions.lesson_line: A spring comes late, after the range has had time to form.

wrong.On the first day of the range: A floor has to form first. ChartSchool, Fraser and Pruden all put the spring late.
wrong.After the range top breaks: That is after the range. ChartSchool and Pruden put the spring late within the range.
wrong.At any point; timing is random: There is a pattern. ChartSchool, Fraser and Pruden all say a spring usually comes late in the range.

questions.simple: A spring usually comes late in the range, after the floor has had time to form.

questions.q: The stop on a spring goes a few cents under the spring low.
questions.why: True. Our card puts the stop a few cents under the spring low, the lowest low of the dip. The same goes for a test entry. Our rulebook keeps a stop a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it. Fraser also places stops under the low of the spring day.
questions.lesson_line: Stop a few cents under the spring low.
questions.simple: True, the stop goes a few cents under the lowest point of the dip, not right on it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62)

questions.q: How tall is a spring's range, floor to top?
questions.why: 6% to 20%, measured from the floor to the top. That band is on our setup card. A range over 20% is not ruled out; it grades lower. A range much tighter than 6% falls short of it.
questions.lesson_line: A spring range is 6% to 20% tall.

wrong.1% to 3%: Too small. Our card asks for a range 6% to 20% tall, floor to top.
wrong.30% to 50%: Over 20% grades lower. This is far past it.
wrong.3% to 6%: Our card's band is 6% to 20%, floor to top. This sits under it.

questions.simple: A spring's range should be 6% to 20% tall, from the floor to the top.

reasons: proposed card criterion, the owner's review pending

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: On our card, a dip over ___ ATR under the floor is a shakeout that grades lower.
questions.why: 1. On our card a dip over 1 ATR under the floor is a shakeout, and it grades lower. A full spring dips at least 0.1 ATR and at most about 1 ATR. Over 2 ATR is a breakdown, not a spring.
questions.lesson_line: A real undercut, but no deeper than about 1 ATR.
questions.simple: Over 1 ATR under the floor, the dip is a shakeout that grades lower.

reasons: proposed card criterion (spr.dip_depth), the owner's review pending

questions.q: Our card still counts a dip of 3 ATR under the floor as a spring.
questions.why: False. Our card calls a dip of over 2 ATR under the floor a breakdown, not a spring. Over 1 ATR it is already a shakeout that grades lower. Fraser names a complete breakdown his number 1 spring, and says it should not be bought.
questions.lesson_line: Past 2 ATR under the floor, it is a breakdown.
questions.simple: False. Past 2 ATR under the floor our card calls it a breakdown, not a spring.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting the owner's review (the ATR bands)

questions.q: What RS rating do we ask for in a spring?
choices: An RS rating of 80 or more
An RS rating of 20 or less
questions.answer: An RS rating of 80 or more
questions.why: An RS rating of 80 or more. We buy leaders: RS 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. The card asks the same of a spring, and adds that the stock is stronger than the market through the range. Only parabolic and mean-reversion trades are exempt from the leader rule.
questions.lesson_line: A spring belongs to a leader, RS 80 or more.

wrong.An RS rating of 20 or less: That is a weak stock. A spring belongs to a leader, RS 80 or more.
wrong.An RS rating near 50: An average stock is not a leader. The bar is 80.
wrong.None; any stock will do: The leader rule applies to springs. Only parabolic and mean-reversion trades are exempt.

questions.simple: An RS rating of 80 or more, because we buy springs only in leaders that are stronger than the market.

questions.q: The reclaim day should close in the upper half of that day's own high-low range.
questions.why: True. Our card asks for close quality: the reclaim day closes in the upper half of its own range, high to low. A close back under the spring low is the opposite case, and it is not bought.
questions.lesson_line: A good reclaim closes in the upper half.
questions.simple: True, a good reclaim day closes in the top half of its own high to low range.

reasons: proposed card criterion (spr.reclaim_close), the owner's review pending

questions.q: Which market readings fit a spring best?
questions.why: Green or Yellow. The card says springs want a Green or Yellow market. The reading is a guide: Green means full risk per grade, Yellow smaller and fewer. In Orange we take only A+ setups, and in Red we are mostly cash and shorts.
questions.lesson_line: Springs fit Green or Yellow markets best.

wrong.Orange or Red, any grade: Orange takes only A+ setups, and Red is mostly cash and shorts. A spring's home is Green or Yellow.
wrong.Any reading, the chart decides: A clean chart does not override the reading. The card names Green or Yellow for springs.
wrong.Red, when fear runs highest: Red means mostly cash and shorts for us. The card names Green or Yellow for springs.

questions.simple: Green or Yellow, because the card names those two readings as the home of a spring.

questions.q: What makes a range flat?
choices: Its closes drift under 1/4 the height
It makes a higher high each week
questions.answer: Its closes drift under 1/4 the height
questions.why: Its closes drift less than a quarter of the range height. That is our card's test for flat: no clear slope. Height is a separate test, 6% to 20% from floor to top. Quiet volume does not make a range flat; flat is about price.
questions.lesson_line: Flat means no clear slope.

wrong.It makes a higher high each week: That is a slope up, a trend. Flat means no clear slope.
wrong.It stands 6% to 20% tall: That is our height test. Flat is about slope: the closes drift less than a quarter of the height.
wrong.Its volume nearly dries up: Flat describes the slope of price, not the volume.

questions.simple: A range is flat when its closes drift less than a quarter of the range height.

reasons: proposed card criterion (spr.flat), the owner's review pending

questions.q: A spring buy is fine two days before an earnings report.
questions.why: False. We make no new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report, and two days out is inside that window. The rule is about new buys only. A trade already up 5R may be held through the report.
questions.lesson_line: No new buy within 3 days of a report.
questions.simple: False. Two days out is inside the 3 days before a report, when we make no new buys.

questions.q: Pruden writes that Wyckoff says to buy the breakout over the range top.
questions.why: False. Pruden writes that, according to Wyckoff, you should not buy breakouts. A false breakout leaves you open to a swift move the other way. Our card buys a spring at the floor, on the reclaim after the undercut.
questions.lesson_line: A spring is bought at the floor, not on the breakout.
questions.simple: False. Pruden writes that Wyckoff warned against buying breakouts, and we buy a spring at the floor.

deeper.counter: The app's scanner plan mixes the two: a buy over the top, with the stop under the spring low. Our card rejects it for a spring: a median 12.5% stop, and 1% reached 3R. A spring is bought at the floor, with the stop a few cents under the spring low.

reasons: the Wyckoff line rests on one publisher (Pruden), so it is asked as his
the floor entry rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting the owner's review (spr.not_breakout_entry)

questions.q: Floor 91.25, top 100.68. How tall is the range, as a percent of the floor?
questions.why: 10.3%. Height is the top minus the floor, divided by the floor: (100.68 - 91.25) / 91.25 = 10.3%. That sits inside our card's 6% to 20% band. Our scan measures it the same way: GIS's 21.30 to 23.30 shelf is 9.4%.
questions.lesson_line: Height is top minus floor, over the floor.
questions.simple: The range is 10.3% tall, which sits inside the 6% to 20% band.

reasons: proposed card criterion (spr.range_height), the owner's review pending

questions.q: The floor is 150.00, ATR is 3.00 and the spring low is 149.10. How deep is the dip, in ATR?
questions.why: 0.3 ATR. Take the dollars under the floor, 150.00 minus 149.10, and divide by the ATR, 3.00. The card's spring dips at least 0.1 ATR and at most about 1 ATR, so 0.3 is a real but shallow undercut. Fraser's shallow number 3 spring also comes on modest volume, which this question does not give.
questions.lesson_line: Dollars under the floor, divided by the ATR.
questions.simple: 0.3 ATR, because you divide the dollars under the floor by the ATR of 3.00.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting the owner's review (0.1 to 1 ATR)

questions.q: Fraser calls a shallow penetration of the prior low on modest volume what?
questions.why: A number 3 spring. Fraser: a shallow penetration of the prior low on modest volume, which can be bought immediately. His number 2 goes further below on expanded volume and then needs a test. His number 1 is a complete breakdown, never bought. ChartSchool and Pruden also favor a quiet spring. These numbers are Fraser's names, not a volume cutoff we teach.
questions.lesson_line: Fraser's number 3: shallow, on modest volume, and bought at once.

wrong.A test on high volume: A test comes after the spring. A successful test typically makes a higher low on lesser volume.
wrong.A number 1 spring: Fraser's number 1 is a complete breakdown that should not be bought, not a shallow dip.
wrong.A number 2 spring: Fraser's number 2 goes further below the low on expanded volume, then needs a test.

questions.simple: Fraser calls a shallow dip on modest volume a number 3 spring, and he says it can be bought right away.

deeper.trap: Fraser's numbers run backwards: number 1 is the deepest and the worst, a breakdown not to buy, and number 3 is the shallow one you can buy. And quiet is not settled. Taylor, a CMT member, wants volume on the spring quite high, the higher the better. Treat the volume read as the Wyckoff school's view, not a fact.

reasons: tied to the held volume decision D-006

questions.q: Our card skips a spring that closes back under its spring low before you buy.
questions.why: True. Our card lists a close back under the spring low, before the buy, as a reason not to buy. So does a dip that keeps going, over 2 ATR on heavy volume. Fraser calls that kind of complete breakdown one that should not be bought.
questions.lesson_line: A close back under the spring low means no buy.
questions.simple: True. A close back under the spring low before the buy cancels the trade.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting the owner's review (spr.inv_close_under_low)

questions.q: Besides the floor, what does a spring often undercut?
questions.why: The 20-day or the 50-day. Our card says the spring often undercuts those averages too. The 200-day is a different matter: below it is a hard no for stocks. A spring is a small dip under a flat floor, not a collapse.
questions.lesson_line: A spring can dip through the 20-day or 50-day. Below the 200-day is a hard no for stocks.

wrong.The 200-day average: Our card names the 20-day or 50-day. Below the 200-day is a hard no for stocks.
wrong.A new multi-year low: A spring dips at most about 1 ATR under a flat floor. It is not a collapse to a new low.
wrong.Nothing but the floor: Our card says the spring often undercuts the 20-day or 50-day too.

questions.simple: It often dips under the 20-day or 50-day too, but below the 200-day is a hard no for stocks.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26) and sits beside the held D-009

questions.q: Any dip under a recent low counts as a spring, even with no range behind it.
questions.why: False. A falling stock makes a new low every day. With no real range behind the dip, that is not a spring.
questions.lesson_line: No range, no spring.

questions.q: What is it?
questions.story: A stock rests in a flat 8-week range, 8% tall, with four touches of the floor. One day it dips 0.3 ATR under the floor and closes back inside, in the upper half of the day's range.
questions.why: A spring. The range is flat and 8% tall, inside the card's 6% to 20%. The dip went 0.3 ATR under the floor, between the card's 0.1 and about 1 ATR. It closed back inside, in the upper half of the day's range. A breakdown needs over 2 ATR, and a 2B has one swing low, not four touches.
questions.lesson_line: Flat range, shallow dip, strong close: a spring.

wrong.A flat-base breakout: A breakout goes over the top. This stock dipped under the floor.
wrong.A breakdown of the floor: A breakdown goes over 2 ATR under the floor. This dip was 0.3 ATR and closed back inside.
wrong.A 2B of a single low: A 2B's level is one swing low. This floor is flat, with four touches.

questions.simple: A spring, because a flat range got a shallow dip that closed back inside and high on the day.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting the owner's review (height, depth, close)

questions.q: Is this a spring?
questions.story: A stock makes a new low every day for two weeks. Then it ticks up and closes above yesterday's low.
questions.why: No. A spring needs a real range behind the dip, and its floor is a flat level. A stock that makes a new low every day has no floor, so a bounce over yesterday's low is not a spring. Volume is not the issue here. The missing range decides it.
questions.lesson_line: A spring needs a floor. A falling stock has none.

wrong.Yes; it bounced back: A bounce in a downtrend is not a spring. There is no floor to reclaim.
wrong.No; volume is wrong: Volume is not the problem. The missing range is.
wrong.Yes; any dip counts: A spring needs a flat range behind the undercut.

questions.simple: No, because a stock falling to a new low every day has no flat floor to dip under.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting the owner's review (spr.inv_no_range)

questions.q: Is this a spring?
choices: No; the dip was too slow
Yes; six days is a deep test
questions.story: A stock closes under its range floor for six sessions in a row, then closes back inside.
questions.answer: No; the dip was too slow
questions.why: No. Pruden defines a spring as a move below support that quickly reverses back into the range. Taylor calls slower violations that fail washouts or bear traps. Six closes under the floor is not quick. This lesson keys only the quick snap back, not an exact count of days.
questions.lesson_line: A spring snaps back. Six weak closes is not a snap.

wrong.Yes; it closed back inside: Closing back inside is part of it. The reversal also has to be quick.
wrong.Yes; six days is a deep test: A test comes after a spring. Six closes under is a slow violation.
wrong.No; it must hold the 50-day: Nothing here says where the 50-day is, and a spring often undercuts the 20-day or 50-day too.

questions.simple: No, because a spring snaps back fast, and six closes under the floor is a slow slide.

reasons: the reclaim window is a held decision (D-005); only 'quickly reverses' is keyed

questions.q: Spring, shakeout or breakdown?
choices: A breakdown; do not buy it
A U&R of a rising average
questions.story: The floor is 359.50. The dip goes 1.34 ATR under it, with one close under, then back inside the next day.
questions.why: A shakeout; grade it lower. The card's spring dips at most about 1 ATR. Over 1 ATR is a shakeout that grades lower, and over 2 ATR is a breakdown. At 1.34 ATR this sits in the middle band. COST went 1.34 ATR under the 359.50 floor, made 0.52R and was stopped.
questions.lesson_line: Between 1 and 2 ATR deep, grade lower.

wrong.A U&R of a rising average: The level here is a flat floor, not a rising average.
wrong.A clean spring; full grade: A clean spring dips about 1 ATR or less under the floor. This one went 1.34 ATR.
wrong.A breakdown; do not buy it: A breakdown is over 2 ATR under the floor. This dip was 1.34 ATR.

questions.simple: A shakeout that grades lower, because 1.34 ATR is past the 1 ATR spring limit but short of a 2 ATR breakdown.

deeper.example: COST: the floor was 359.50 and the probe went 1.34 ATR under it. The buy was 361.30 with the stop at 352.41, a 2.46% stop. It made 0.52R and was stopped. A deeper dip puts the stop further from the buy.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting the owner's review (1 and 2 ATR bands)

questions.q: Where does the stop go?
questions.story: The floor is 38.00. The spring low is 37.62. You buy the reclaim at 38.10.
questions.why: A few cents under 37.62, the spring low. Our card puts the stop there, not on the old floor at 38.00. Our rulebook keeps it a few cents under the low, not exactly on it. Fraser also places stops under the low of the spring day. It is a real stop order with the broker.
questions.lesson_line: The stop goes under the spring low, not the old floor.

wrong.Far below, near 35.00: That is a wide stop, far past the spring low. The line is the spring low, a few cents under it.
wrong.A few cents under 38.00: 38.00 is the old floor, above the 37.62 spring low. The stop goes a few cents under the spring low.
wrong.Right on 38.00, the floor: 38.00 sits above the 37.62 spring low, so it is not under the dip. The stop goes a few cents under the spring low.

questions.simple: Put the stop a few cents under 37.62, the spring low, not on the old floor.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62, D41)

questions.q: You buy at 62.50 with the stop at 61.30. How far is the stop, as a percent of the buy?
questions.why: 1.92%. Stop distance is the buy minus the stop, divided by the buy: (62.50 - 61.30) / 62.50 = 1.92%. That is inside the 1-3% we prefer for stops.
questions.lesson_line: Stop distance in percent: buy minus stop, divided by the buy.
questions.simple: The stop is 1.92% under the buy, which sits inside the range we prefer for stops.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A13) and the held stop-width decision D-022

questions.q: Buy the spring?
choices: Pass; Red is mostly cash and shorts
Yes; the stock itself is clean
Yes, at half size with a tighter stop
questions.story: A clean spring in a stock above its 200-day. The market reading is Red.
questions.answer: Pass; Red is mostly cash and shorts
questions.why: Pass. In a Red market our rulebook says mostly cash and shorts. Our card takes springs in a Green or Yellow market. A clean chart does not override the reading, and a smaller size does not either. Shorting it is out too: we short only below the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: A clean spring in a Red market is still a pass.

wrong.Yes; the stock itself is clean: A clean chart does not beat the market reading. Red is mostly cash and shorts.
wrong.Yes, at half size with a tighter stop: A smaller size does not change the reading. Springs are Green or Yellow trades.
wrong.Pass; short the stock instead: Our shorts go only below the 200-day, unless parabolic. This stock is above it.

questions.simple: Pass, because in a Red market we hold mostly cash and shorts, and springs are Green or Yellow trades.

deeper.trap: The trap is a perfect chart. The market reading comes before the chart. Our card takes springs in Green or Yellow, and Red means mostly cash and shorts.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F65) and the card's market row

questions.q: What does the index tell you?
choices: The market turn has not come
Size up; the leader is stronger
The turn is in; QQQ sprang today
questions.story: A leader springs off its range floor. QQQ sprang the same day. Before you buy, QQQ closes back under its own spring low.
questions.answer: The market turn has not come
questions.why: The market turn has not come. QQQ's own spring failed when it closed back under its low. ChartSchool's Wyckoff step is to time your commitment with a turn in the stock market index. In one AAPL case from our data, QQQ sprang the same day and failed too.
questions.lesson_line: Check the index before you buy a leader's spring.

wrong.Nothing; only the stock matters: The index matters. Wyckoff times the buy with a turn in the stock market index.
wrong.Size up; the leader is stronger: A failing index spring is a warning, not a reason to size up.
wrong.The turn is in; QQQ sprang today: QQQ's spring failed when it closed back under its low. Its own spring had not held.

questions.simple: The market has not turned, because the index's own spring just failed.

deeper.example: AAPL and QQQ sprang on the same day in our data, and both failed. The scan scored the QQQ spring 0.0R. The index's own spring had not held, so the leader had no market turn to ride.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting the owner's review (spr.index_sprung)

questions.q: What do you take from it?
choices: The setup is broken; quit it
questions.story: A 0.16 ATR dip on light volume in a 40-day range with three touches. A 1% stop. It is stopped on the entry day with no profit.
questions.why: A spring that fails usually fails at once. 41% broke their low before any test came. The stop under the spring low is the exit.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is the trade, not a formality.

wrong.The setup is broken; quit it: One failed spring is the cost of the setup. 41% broke their low before any test.
wrong.The stop was too tight: The stop sat under the spring low, where it belongs.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Skip it; take it off the list
Buy it; the shape is textbook perfect
Buy a half size until it settles
Keep it on the list for later
questions.story: A textbook spring in a leader. Then a buyout report comes out.
questions.answer: Skip it; take it off the list
questions.why: Skip it. Our hard rule: as soon as there is buyout news, the stock comes off the list. The card says the same, skip on buyout news. A perfect chart does not change that, and off the list means it is not kept for later either.
questions.lesson_line: Buyout news takes the stock off the list.

wrong.Buy it; the shape is textbook perfect: A perfect shape does not beat the buyout rule. Buyout news takes the stock off the list.
wrong.Buy a half size until it settles: Off the list means no buy at any size. Buyout news takes the stock off the list.
wrong.Keep it on the list for later: Off the list means off. As soon as there is buyout news, the stock comes off the list.

questions.simple: Skip it, because our hard rule takes a stock off the list as soon as buyout news appears.

reasons: rests on the owner's published hard rule (u04) and the card

questions.q: At entry, how far above its 10-day average may a stock be?
questions.why: No more than 10%. Too stretched to buy: we skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average. The card applies the same line at the spring entry. It measures the distance from the average, not from the floor.
questions.lesson_line: Too stretched above the 10-day means skip.

wrong.No more than 1%: That is far tighter than the rule.
wrong.No more than 25%: The rule is 10%. A stock 25% above its 10-day is far too stretched.
wrong.There is no limit: There is a limit: 10% above the 10-day.

questions.simple: No more than 10%, because a long more than 10% above its 10-day average is too stretched to buy.

questions.q: What is wrong with that plan?
choices: The stop is far from the entry
questions.story: The scanner says to buy the range-top breakout and put the stop under the spring low.
questions.answer: The stop is far from the entry
questions.why: The stop is far from the entry. That plan had a median 12.5% stop and only 1% reached 3R. Wyckoff also says not to buy breakouts.
questions.lesson_line: Buy at the floor. A breakout buy leaves the stop far away.

wrong.The stop is too tight: It is the opposite. The stop sits far under a breakout entry.
wrong.Breakouts never work: Some do. The problem is the distance to the stop.
wrong.The range is too flat: A flat range is what we want.

questions.q: A spring still under 1R after 10 sessions is sold.
questions.why: True. Our time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money. The card uses the same rule for springs. It is a rule about time, separate from the price stop under the spring low.
questions.lesson_line: Ten sessions under 1R, sell.
questions.simple: True. A spring that has not reached 1R after 10 sessions is sold to free the money.

questions.q: If a spring breaks its low, add to the position to average down.
questions.why: False. The stop under the spring low is the exit, so a broken low means you are out. We buy the full size at one price with one stop, with no adding. A spring that fails usually fails at once, so the stop is the trade, not a chance to buy more.
questions.lesson_line: A broken spring low means out, not more.
questions.simple: False. When a spring breaks its low the stop takes you out, and we never add to a trade.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, A5)

questions.q: What do you do at 3R?
choices: Hold past 68.80; no sale before day 3
Sell a third at 68.80; move stop to 64
Sell half at 68.80; stop stays put
Add to the winner at 68.80 on strength
questions.story: You bought at 64.00 with a stop at 62.40. On the buy day itself, price runs to 68.80, which is 3R.
questions.answer: Hold past 68.80; no sale before day 3
questions.why: Hold. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R. We very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy and usually wait until day 3 at the earliest. Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R, is often best.
questions.lesson_line: The first sell is a judgment, and it rarely comes on day 1.

wrong.Sell half at 68.80; stop stays put: Selling on day 1 is rare. The first sell waits for day 3 at the earliest.
wrong.Sell a third at 68.80; move stop to 64: The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R. Day 1 is rarely the day to sell.
wrong.Add to the winner at 68.80 on strength: We never add. The full size goes on at one price with one stop.

questions.simple: Hold. We rarely sell on day 1, and the first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R.

deeper.counter: A day-based push can run far past 3R. A 3, 5 or 7 day push may be 10, 12 or 20R, so a fixed third at 3R can leave most of the move behind.

questions.q: How do we trail the rest of a spring?
choices: A fixed 3% stop under the entry
Keep it under the spring low, unmoved
questions.why: Under the 21-day, or the 10-day if it runs fast. Our default trail is the 10-day average for fast movers and the 21-day for steadier ones. We sell on a close below it. The card says most springs use the 21-day. The trail is for the last third, after the earlier sells.
questions.lesson_line: Trail the 21-day, or the 10-day when it runs.

wrong.Under the 200-day average line: Our trail is the 10-day or the 21-day average, not the 200-day.
wrong.A fixed 3% stop under the entry: A fixed stop does not follow the move. About 3% is where the first stop usually sits, not a trail.
wrong.Keep it under the spring low, unmoved: That is the first stop. After the trims, the last third trails under the 21-day or the 10-day.

questions.simple: Under the 21-day for most springs, or the 10-day for fast movers, selling on a close below it.

questions.q: In our scan, about how far was the range top from a reclaim entry, at the median?
questions.why: About 4.8R, the median in our scan, and 3R or more 72% of the time. The range top is the first resistance, so 3R usually comes at or before it. It is a median, not a promise: some range tops sit closer than 3R.
questions.lesson_line: The range top is the first resistance, often past 3R.

wrong.About 3R, right at the mark: The median in our scan is 4.8R, past the 3R mark. 72% of the time it is 3R or more.
wrong.About 1.6R, before the 3R mark: The median is 4.8R, and 72% of the time it is 3R or more.
wrong.About 9.6R, far past that mark: The median in our scan is 4.8R, not 9.6R.

questions.simple: In our scan the range top sat a median 4.8R away, so 3R usually comes first.

reasons: a scan statistic that a recheck can change

questions.q: What now?
questions.story: You bought at 100.00 with a stop at 98.00. The stock gaps down and the first 30-minute low is 95.00.
questions.why: Out. On a gap through the stop, the low of the first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop. The ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out. One R here is 100.00 minus 98.00. The 95.00 low is 2.5R under the buy, past the 2R cap.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop is capped at 2R. Past that, leave.

wrong.Hold; it should bounce back: The stop is the exit. On a gap, the 30-minute low and the 2R cap decide.
wrong.Buy more at 95.00 to average: We never add. The full size goes on at one price with one stop.
wrong.New stop at 95.00, the 30-min low: That is the gap rule without its ceiling. The loss here is 2.5R, past 2R, so you get out.

questions.simple: Get out, because the gap took the loss to 2.5R, past our 2R cap.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20, A4)

questions.q: What does our plan say to do at the open?
choices: Make the planned sell at the open
Wait for 60.00 to make the sell
Add more at 57.50 on the gap
questions.story: You bought at 50.00 with a stop at 48.00. On day 3 you plan your first sell at 3R, 56.00. The stock opens at 57.50.
questions.answer: Make the planned sell at the open
questions.why: Make the planned sell at the open. You planned to sell at 56.00, which is 3R, and the day opened at 57.50, past it. Our rule: if a stock opens above a sell level, take that sell at the open. The first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later.
questions.lesson_line: If it opens past a sell level, sell at the open.

wrong.Hold everything and trail it: The plan sells at 56.00 first. The trail is only for the part left after the sell.
wrong.Add more at 57.50 on the gap: We never add. The full size goes on at one price with one stop.
wrong.Wait for 60.00 to make the sell: You planned to sell at 56.00. A sell level the day opens past is taken at the open.

questions.simple: Make the planned sell at the open, because the stock opened past your 56.00 level.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F63, B19)

questions.q: Do the sources agree on volume at the spring?
choices: Yes; all of them want loud volume
questions.why: No. Fraser's number 3 spring, the one he buys at once, is a shallow dip on modest volume. He wants a loud spring tested first. Taylor says volume on the spring is typically quite high, the higher the better. The sources disagree, so this lesson keys no volume rule as ours.
questions.lesson_line: The sources disagree on volume. Know both views.

wrong.Yes; all of them want loud volume: Fraser buys a spring on modest volume.
wrong.Yes; all want quiet volume: Taylor says volume on the spring is typically quite high.
wrong.No; Fraser loud, Taylor quiet: That is backwards. Taylor wants high volume on the spring, and Fraser buys the modest-volume one at once.

questions.simple: No, because Fraser buys a quiet spring at once while Taylor says the louder the spring the better.

deeper.trap: Do not turn one author's view into a rule. Fraser sorts springs by volume: a quiet number 3 he buys at once, a loud number 2 he waits to see tested. Taylor wants the loud one. This lesson keys only that they disagree.

reasons: volume is a held decision (D-006); only the disagreement is keyed

questions.q: After a loud, deep spring, what does the Wyckoff school wait for?
choices: A test that makes a higher low
A gap up on heavy volume
The next earnings report to pass
questions.answer: A test that makes a higher low
questions.why: A test that makes a higher low. Fraser says high volume springs need to be tested in the following days or weeks. ChartSchool adds that a successful test typically makes a higher low on lesser volume. Pruden calls the later test a better place to buy than the spring itself. This is the Wyckoff school's view, not a UCT entry rule.
questions.lesson_line: After a loud spring, wait for the test.

wrong.A gap up on heavy volume: The sources wait for a test, not a gap.
wrong.The 200-day to turn upward: The line is not the test. The test is a pullback that holds above the spring low.
wrong.The next earnings report to pass: Our rule is no new buy within 3 days of a report. A report is not the test.

questions.simple: A test, because a loud spring must be tested, and a good test holds a higher low.

deeper.trap: A test that breaks the spring low is not a test that held. Taylor says the spring low should not be violated by any significant degree, or the structure is invalidated. The good test holds above it, on lighter volume.

reasons: which entry we teach is a held decision (D-003); keyed as the school's view

questions.q: Which range is the better place for a spring?
choices: A base after a long decline
A range right after an IPO
questions.why: A pause after a rise. The 60 sessions before the range rose, a reaccumulation pause, is preferred to a base after a decline.
questions.lesson_line: Prefer a pause after a rise to a base after a fall.

wrong.A base after a long decline: That is the classic accumulation spring. We prefer a pause after a rise.
wrong.A range under the 200-day: No longs under the 200-day unless a parabolic long.
wrong.A range right after an IPO: A new issue has no rise or floor history to read.

questions.q: Buy the spring?
questions.story: A textbook spring in a stock with an RS rating of 55, in a weak group.
questions.why: Skip. A spring is bought in a leader, RS 80 or more. Only parabolic and mean-reversion trades are exempt.
questions.lesson_line: No leader, no spring.

wrong.Buy; the shape is textbook: A textbook shape in a weak stock is still a pass.
wrong.Buy; springs are exempt: Only parabolic and mean-reversion trades are exempt from the leader rule.
wrong.Buy at half size: Size does not fix a weak stock.

questions.q: Buy it or pass?
choices: Buy at half size, tight stop
questions.story: A textbook spring in a stock under a flat 200-day, after a nine-month decline.
questions.why: Pass. Below the 200-day is a hard no for stocks, and this stock is under it. Only an index or a levered ETF may go under it, on a reversal extension or a parabolic long. The rule is about where price sits, not how clean the pattern is. Our card also prefers a range after a rise, not a base after a decline.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day, no stock long, however clean the spring looks.

wrong.Buy now; a textbook spring: A textbook shape under the 200-day still breaks the rule.
wrong.Buy at half size, tight stop: Half size does not fix a rule break.
wrong.Pass; the 200-day must rise: Our rule is about price, not slope. The stock is under the line, and that alone rules out a long.

questions.simple: Pass, because we take no stock longs under the 200-day line, however clean the spring looks.

deeper.trap: The trap is the textbook shape. After a long decline a spring can look perfect on its own chart. Our 200-day rule is hard for stocks: no long below the line. The shape never overrides the line.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26) beside the held D-009

questions.q: What does our card say about its grade?
choices: Lower; the range is over 20% tall
Full grade; the dip is shallow
Higher; a tall range is strong
Pass; too tall to be a spring
questions.story: A spring comes from a flat range 22% tall. The dip is 0.4 ATR under the floor and closes back inside.
questions.answer: Lower; the range is over 20% tall
questions.why: Lower. The card wants a range 6% to 20% tall, and over 20% grades lower. The dip of 0.4 ATR is fine, inside the 0.1 to about 1 ATR band. So it is still a spring, just a weaker one. The cue is a guide, since our rulebook keeps grading discretionary.
questions.lesson_line: A range over 20% tall costs grade, even with a clean dip.

wrong.Full grade; the dip is shallow: The dip is fine, but a range over 20% tall grades lower.
wrong.Higher; a tall range is strong: The card grades a range over 20% tall lower, not higher.
wrong.Pass; too tall to be a spring: The card grades it lower. It does not rule it out.

questions.simple: Lower, because the card grades a range over 20% tall lower, even when the dip is fine.

deeper.trap: The trap is to call it a pass. The card grades a range over 20% tall lower; it does not throw it out. The 0.4 ATR dip sits inside the 0.1 to about 1 ATR band.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting the owner's review (20% height)
grading is discretionary (E50); the cue is credited to the card

questions.q: Which setup is this?
questions.story: A stock dips just under its rising 50-day for a day and closes back above it. No flat range sits behind it.
questions.why: An undercut and rally. A U&R's level can be one swing low, a rising average or a prior high. A spring's floor is a flat level, and this story has no flat range, only a rising 50-day. Name the level first: a flat floor means a spring, a rising average means a U&R.
questions.lesson_line: A flat floor is a spring. A rising average is a U&R.

wrong.A capitulation flush: A capitulation is a 2 ATR flush on 2x volume. This dip went just under the average.
wrong.A spring off the 50-day: A spring's floor is a flat level with a range behind it. A rising average is a U&R level.
wrong.A 2B of one swing low: A 2B's level is one swing low. Here the level is a rising average.

questions.simple: It is an undercut and rally, because the level is a rising average, not a flat floor.

deeper.trap: The trap is calling every undercut a spring. Both dip under a level and close back above it. The difference is the level: a spring needs a flat floor with a range behind it, while a U&R can use a rising average, one swing low or a prior high.

reasons: rests on the card's lookalike tells (house)

questions.q: Name each trade.
questions.story: Two traders watch the same flat range. Trader A buys the reclaim at the floor. Trader B buys through the top.
questions.why: A: spring. B: flat base. A spring is bought at the floor on the reclaim after the undercut, with the stop under the dip. A flat base is bought through the top of the range, with the stop under the breakout day's low. Same range, two setups, two stops.
questions.lesson_line: Floor reclaim is a spring. Top breakout is a flat base.

wrong.A: base. B: spring: It is the other way round. The floor buy is the spring.
wrong.Both are springs: A spring is bought at the floor, not through the top.
wrong.Both are flat bases: A flat base is bought through the top, not at the floor.

questions.simple: A bought a spring at the floor, and B bought a flat base through the top of the same range.

deeper.counter: Same range, different stop. The spring buyer's stop sits a few cents under the spring low, near the floor. The flat-base buyer's stop sits under the breakout day's low, near the top. Mixing the two, a top buy with a floor stop, is the plan the card rejects.

reasons: the reclaim entry is a held decision (D-003); keyed as the card's lookalike tell

questions.q: Which setup is this?
questions.story: After a short dip with no range behind it, a stock trades under the prior day's low. In the same session it closes back above the prior day's close.
questions.why: An Oops Reversal. On our card an Oops breaks yesterday's low and reclaims yesterday's close on one candle. A spring breaks the floor of a range, and this short dip has no range behind it.
questions.lesson_line: Yesterday's low is an Oops. The range floor is a spring.

wrong.A spring low: A spring breaks the floor of a range. This broke only the prior day's low.
wrong.A capitulation: A capitulation is a 2 ATR flush on 2x volume. A short dip is not one.
wrong.A failed break: A failed breakout is a break above a level that falls back. This broke a low.

questions.simple: It is an Oops Reversal, because it broke only the prior day's low, not the floor of a range.

reasons: rests on the card's lookalike tells (house)

questions.q: Which setup is this?
questions.story: A leader falls in a straight line. Then it drops 2.5 ATR in one day on twice its usual volume, under all its fast averages.
questions.why: A capitulation. Our card calls a 2 ATR flush on 2x volume under the fast averages a capitulation, once its burst boxes are checked. This one fell 2.5 ATR on twice the usual volume after a straight-line fall. A spring goes only 0.1 to 1 ATR under a flat floor.
questions.lesson_line: A big flush after a straight fall is a capitulation.

wrong.An Oops Reversal: An Oops breaks yesterday's low and reclaims yesterday's close on one candle. Nothing here reclaims.
wrong.A shakeout spring: Over 1 ATR is a shakeout, but over 2 ATR is a breakdown, not a spring. This dropped 2.5 ATR.
wrong.An undercut and rally: A U&R undercuts a level, such as a rising average, and rallies back. This was a straight-line flush.

questions.simple: It is a capitulation: a 2.5 ATR flush on 2x volume under the fast averages, far past a spring's 1 ATR.

deeper.trap: Depth is the tell. A spring's dip is 0.1 to 1 ATR under a flat floor. Over 1 ATR our card calls it a shakeout that grades lower. Over 2 ATR is a breakdown, and a 2 ATR flush on 2x volume under the fast averages is a capitulation, a different setup with different rules.

reasons: rests on the card's lookalike tells (house)

questions.q: What do you do now?
choices: Done; the stop was the trade
Buy it back bigger right away
Move the stop under the next low
Hold; it may close back inside
questions.story: You bought a spring in a range 17.9% tall, after a 73% run. The same day it fell through your stop under the spring low.
questions.answer: Done; the stop was the trade
questions.why: The trade is done. The stop under the spring low is the exit. A spring that fails usually fails at once: in our scan 41% broke their low before any test came. After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out is the cost of the setup.

wrong.Move the stop under the next low: The stop only moves up, never down or wider. The stop was hit, so the trade is over.
wrong.Buy it back bigger right away: A new buy needs the setup to trigger again, as a new trade with its own stop.
wrong.Hold; it may close back inside: The stop is the exit, and it was hit. Every position has a real stop order with the broker.

questions.simple: The trade is over, because the stop under the spring low was the plan.

deeper.example: The numbers come from TSLA in our scan: a 17.9% tall range, near the 20% limit, after a 73% run in the prior 60 sessions. A tall range after a big run sits at the edge of the card. When a spring fails, the stop doing its job is the plan.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, B21)
fixed before (a dossier quote was wrong against the bars)

questions.q: Entry 142.00, stop 140.00, old range top 148.00. How many R is the top away?
questions.why: 3.0R. One R is the entry minus the stop: 142.00 - 140.00, or $2. The top is (148.00 - 142.00) / 2 = 3.0R above the entry. That matches the 3-1 gain our DELL plan expected by the time the breakout buyers step in.
questions.lesson_line: Range top over the entry, divided by the risk.
questions.simple: The top is 3R away, because the $2 risk fits three times into the climb to 148.00.

deeper.counter: Here the top is on the near side. In our scan the range top sat a median 4.8R from the reclaim entry. When the top is only 3R away, the first resistance and 3R arrive together, so a first sell near the ceiling is a real option.

reasons: rests on house sources (the DELL plan, the card)

questions.q: In our scan of 3,173 springs, about what share reached 3R before the stop?
questions.why: About a quarter: 27.1% reached 3R and 17.7% reached 5R, and 83.8% were stopped within the window. That is a fixed stop with no trims.
questions.lesson_line: A quarter got to 3R. The stop is the trade.

questions.q: Write the plan: entry, stop, first sell.
choices: Buy over 52.80; stop 47.20; all at top
questions.story: A flat shelf runs from 47.20 to 52.80 with four floor touches. A quiet one-day dip to 46.95, 0.2 ATR under the floor, closes back inside. The next open is 47.40.
questions.why: Buy at the open, 47.40, with the stop a few cents under the 46.95 spring low, not on the 47.20 floor. The first sell is a judgment and comes from day 3 at the earliest, not on day 1.
questions.lesson_line: Entry at the reclaim, stop under the spring low, first sell from day 3.

wrong.Buy over 52.80; stop 47.20; all at top: Buying over the top is the breakout entry. And 47.20 is the old floor, above the 46.95 spring low.
wrong.Buy 47.40; stop 47.20; hold a month: 47.20 is the old floor, above the 46.95 spring low. The stop goes a few cents under the spring low.
wrong.Buy over 52.80; stop 46.92; sell day 3: That buys the breakout over the top with the stop under the spring low. Our card rejects it: a median 12.5% stop, and 1% reached 3R.

questions.simple: Buy at the next open, 47.40, put the stop just under the 46.95 low, and make the first sell from day 3.

deeper.trap: The trap is the breakout plan. Buying over the top at 52.80 with the stop still under the spring low makes a huge stop. Our card says that plan had a median 12.5% stop, and only 1% reached 3R. The spring's edge is the low-risk buy at the floor.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, F62, B19)

questions.q: Hidden ticker. The last bar undercut a recent low and closed back above it. On the pattern alone, take it or pass?
choices: Take it; flat floor, modest dip
Pass; the dip is a breakdown
Take it; the volume was heavy
questions.answer: Take it; flat floor, modest dip
questions.why: Take it. A flat range 7.2% tall with five floor touches. Then one probe 0.75 ATR under the floor closed back inside on 0.96x volume. The dip sits inside our 0.1 to 1 ATR band, far from the over 2 ATR of a breakdown. Take it means a spring worth the plan, not an order at that bar.
questions.lesson_line: A flat floor and a modest dip that snaps back.

wrong.Pass; there is no range: Look again: the floor was touched five times.
wrong.Pass; the dip is a breakdown: A breakdown is over 2 ATR. This probe was 0.75 ATR.
wrong.Take it; the volume was heavy: Volume was 0.96x, about normal, not heavy. The flat floor and the modest dip make this one.

questions.simple: Take it, because the floor is flat and the dip of 0.75 ATR is modest and closed back inside.

deeper.trap: The trap is the deeper probe. After five floor touches this one went three-quarters of an ATR under, which can look like a break. It is still inside the 1 ATR band and closed back in on normal volume. Depth, not drama, decides.

reasons: rests on our own scan's example, not yet reviewed by the owner

questions.q: Hidden ticker. The last bar undercut an old low and closed back above it. Spring or pass?
choices: Pass; one swing low is a 2B
Take it; the dip is shallow
Take it; the floor is flat
Pass; that low is too old to count
questions.answer: Pass; one swing low is a 2B
questions.why: Pass. One swing low, 40 sessions old, set the floor, and price rallied 14% off it. A 2B's level is one swing low; a spring's floor is a flat level. With no flat range to look left at, this is a 2B, not a spring.
questions.lesson_line: A single low is a 2B. A spring needs a flat floor.

wrong.Take it; the dip is shallow: A shallow dip does not make a floor. A spring needs a flat range.
wrong.Take it; the floor is flat: The floor is one swing low, not a flat level.
wrong.Pass; that low is too old to count: Age is not the card's tell here. The floor is one swing low, and that is a 2B's level.

questions.simple: Pass, because one old swing low makes a 2B, while a spring needs a flat floor.

deeper.trap: The trap is a clean undercut. The dip was shallow and closed back above the low, just like a spring. But the level was one swing low that price rallied 14% off, with no flat range behind it. Look left first: no range, no spring.

reasons: tied to the held floor-touch decision D-112

questions.q: What does Wyckoff's step 5 ask of the buyer?
choices: Time your buy with a turn in the index
questions.answer: Time your buy with a turn in the index
questions.why: Time your commitment with a turn in the stock market index. Springs work best when the index itself has just sprung back.
questions.lesson_line: Wait for the index to turn.

wrong.Buy before the index turns: Step 5 says to time your buy with the turn, not ahead of it.
wrong.Ignore the index: The index matters. A failed index spring takes leaders with it.
wrong.Buy only on a Monday: Nothing in the step mentions a weekday.

questions.q: Taylor says the spring low should not be violated by any significant degree.
questions.why: True. In his view the spring low should not be violated by any significant degree, or the structure is invalidated.
questions.lesson_line: A spring that breaks its low is invalid.

questions.q: Pruden calls the spring the first place to buy. What does he say is better?
questions.why: The later secondary test. Pruden says the spring is the first prescribed place to buy and the secondary test is better.
questions.lesson_line: A quiet test can beat the spring itself.

wrong.The breakout over the top: Wyckoff says not to buy breakouts.
wrong.The selling climax: The test comes after the spring, not at a climax.
wrong.Waiting a year: The test comes in the following days or weeks.

questions.q: Which candidate grades higher?
choices: A; the range, dip and close are cleaner
B; the deeper dip shook out more
questions.story: A: a range 8% tall, a dip of 0.3 ATR, a reclaim that closes in the upper half. B: a range 24% tall, a dip of 1.4 ATR, a reclaim that closes mid-range.
questions.answer: A; the range, dip and close are cleaner
questions.why: A. A range over 20% tall grades lower. A dip over 1 ATR is a shakeout that grades lower. A good reclaim closes in the upper half.
questions.lesson_line: Short range, shallow dip, strong close: the higher grade.

wrong.B; the deeper dip shook out more: A dip over 1 ATR is a shakeout, and it grades lower.
wrong.They grade the same: Range height, dip depth and close quality all separate them.
wrong.Neither; both are breakdowns: A breakdown is over 2 ATR. Neither dip is that deep.

questions.q: How does the index's move change the setup?
choices: Stronger; this is the best case
No change; only the stock matters
Pass; the index is still correcting
Weaker; the bounce is used up
questions.story: A leader springs in a flat range. Last week the index dipped under its correction low and closed back above it. The market reading is Green.
questions.answer: Stronger; this is the best case
questions.why: Stronger. Last week's dip and close back above the low was the index's own spring. Our card says a spring is best when the index itself has just sprung back from a correction. The Green reading fits a spring too.
questions.lesson_line: A leader's spring with a turning index is the best case.

wrong.No change; only the stock matters: The index matters. Our card says a spring is best when the index has just sprung back.
wrong.Weaker; the bounce is used up: An index that has just sprung back is the best case for a spring, not a late one.
wrong.Pass; the index is still correcting: The index just sprang back from its correction low. Our card calls that the best case.

questions.simple: Stronger, because a spring is best when the index has just sprung back and the reading is Green.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting the owner's review (spr.index_sprung)

questions.q: Which range is the better spring base?
choices: A; a pause after a rise
B; a base after a fall
questions.story: Range A follows a 31% rise. Range B follows a 13% fall. Both are flat, 12% tall, and above the 200-day.
questions.answer: A; a pause after a rise
questions.why: A. The card prefers the 60 sessions before the range to have risen. That is a reaccumulation pause, Fraser's stepping stone, not a base after a decline. Both ranges pass the other checks: flat, 12% tall inside the 6% to 20% band, and above the 200-day. HWM was such a stepping stone after a 31% run.
questions.lesson_line: Prefer a pause after a rise to a base after a fall.

wrong.B; a base after a fall: A base after a decline is the less preferred prior trend.
wrong.Equal; only the range counts: The prior trend separates them. A pause after a rise is preferred.

questions.simple: A, because a flat pause after a rise is the preferred spring base, not a base after a fall.

deeper.example: HWM: a stepping-stone range after a 31% run, three floor touches and a shallow quiet probe. The range ran from 170.34 to 193.26, 13.5% tall. The buy was 171.85 with the stop at 169.42, and it reached 16.5R at best.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting the owner's review (spr.prior_advance)

questions.q: When does the stop go to breakeven on a spring?
choices: At the first trim, by default
questions.answer: At the first trim, by default
questions.why: At the first trim by default, and anywhere between 2R and 5R. A third comes off at 3R.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven comes with the first trim.

wrong.Never: The stop moves to breakeven between 2R and 5R.
wrong.Before the buy: There is no position yet. Breakeven comes after the first trim.
wrong.At the open each day: The stop only moves up when the rule says so, not each day.

questions.q: What type is this, and what next?
choices: A number 2 spring; wait for the test
questions.story: The dip goes much further under the low on expanded volume. Then it lifts briefly and drops back toward the lows.
questions.answer: A number 2 spring; wait for the test
questions.why: A number 2 spring. It goes further below the low on expanded volume, then lifts and drops back for a test. High volume springs need to be tested first.
questions.lesson_line: A deeper, louder spring waits for its test.

wrong.A number 3 spring; buy now: A number 3 spring is shallow on modest volume. This one is deeper and louder.
wrong.A number 1 spring; buy now: A number 1 spring is a complete breakdown, and it should not be bought.
wrong.A breakout; add: The stock dipped under the low. A breakout goes over the top.

questions.q: Four valid springs lost. Which one had no warning sign?
choices: TSLA; a tall range after a run
questions.why: MSFT. It met every rule and was stopped on the entry day. GOOGL's market, AAPL's index and TSLA's 17.9% range after a 73% run were warnings.
questions.lesson_line: Some good springs still fail. The stop is the trade.

wrong.GOOGL; the market was weak: It was not a Green market, a warning sign.
wrong.AAPL; the index failed: QQQ sprang the same day and failed too, a warning sign.
wrong.TSLA; a tall range after a run: A 17.9% range after a 73% run was a warning sign.

questions.q: After the push to the top of the range, what is the back-up?
choices: A light dip that holds the old top
A heavy drop under the floor
The first dip under the floor
A gap through the range top
questions.answer: A light dip that holds the old top
questions.why: A light dip that holds the old top. After the push to the top of the range, the first light-volume pullback that holds the old top is the back-up. Pruden describes the backup as a narrow reaction on lighter volume that tests the jump. It is not the spring, which dips under the floor.
questions.lesson_line: The back-up is the first light pullback after the push that holds the old top.

wrong.A heavy drop under the floor: That is a breakdown, not a back-up. A back-up is light and holds the old top.
wrong.The first dip under the floor: That is the spring itself. The back-up comes later, after the push to the top.
wrong.A gap through the range top: That is the push. The back-up is the pullback after it.

questions.simple: The back-up is the first light pullback after the push to the top that holds the old top.

questions.q: Fraser calls this a classic place to add. What do we do?
choices: No add; one price, one stop
questions.answer: No add; one price, one stop
questions.why: No add. Fraser calls the back-up a classic place to add. ChartSchool calls a last point of support a place to start or add. Our rule replaced that view: the full size at one price with one stop, and no adding. You hold, and the stop is the exit.
questions.lesson_line: Wyckoff adds at the back-up. We buy once and do not add.

wrong.Add half size, same stop: No adding. The plan is the full size at one price with one stop.
wrong.Double up, raise the stop: The plan has no adds, however the stop moves.
wrong.No add; sell the pullback: The stop is the exit, not a pullback. A light-volume dip that holds the old top is a sign of support.

questions.story: You hold a long from the spring. The stock has pushed to the top of the range and now pulls back on light volume, holding the old top.
questions.simple: Do not add, because we buy the full size once, at one price with one stop.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading the source as our rule. Fraser and ChartSchool both call this pullback a place to add. Our rulebook says the full size at one price with one stop, no adding. Where our rulebook speaks, it beats the textbook.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5) over a web view

questions.q: Does it pass our floors?
choices: No; the share price is under 10
Yes; the dollar volume is big
Half size, with a tight range
questions.answer: No; the share price is under 10
questions.why: No. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. This one trades about $60 million a day, which clears the dollar floor, but 9.40 is under the $10 price floor. Miss either floor and it is a pass.
questions.lesson_line: Two floors: $10 a share and $20 million a day. Miss either and it is a pass.

wrong.Yes; the dollar volume is big: Both floors must pass. The price is under $10.
wrong.Half size, with a tight range: A tight range does not waive a floor, and half size does not either.
wrong.No; 60 million is too low: 60 million clears our 20 million floor. The price is the problem, not the volume.

questions.story: A clean spring shows up in a 9.40 stock that trades about 60 million dollars a day.
questions.simple: No, because the price of 9.40 is under our $10 floor, even though the volume is fine.

questions.q: A stock trades 750,000 shares a day at 24.00. How many dollars a day is that?
questions.why: $18 million a day. Dollar volume is shares times price: 750,000 x 24.00. That is under our $20 million floor, so the stock is off the list, whatever the chart shows.
questions.lesson_line: Check the dollar volume before the pattern. The floor is $20 million a day.
questions.simple: It trades $18 million a day, under the $20 million floor, so it is off the list.

questions.q: Apart from the gap rule, a stop set under the spring low can move up but never lower.
questions.why: True. The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule. On a gap through the stop, the low of the first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop. You get out if that loss passes 2R.
questions.lesson_line: A stop only moves up. The gap rule is the one exception.
questions.simple: True, a stop only moves up, except when a gap opens below it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, B20)

questions.q: What do you do with the stop?
choices: Leave it; the stop never goes lower
Drop it to 50.20 to give it room
Cancel the order and watch the close
Widen it and sell shares to match
questions.answer: Leave it; the stop never goes lower
questions.why: Leave it. The stop is the exit, and it only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is a gap through the stop. The stop stays a real order with the broker, not a level you watch. The size came from 52.40 and 51.10, so a lower stop means more risk than planned.
questions.lesson_line: Leave the stop alone. It moves up, never lower.

wrong.Drop it to 50.20 to give it room: A stop does not go lower or wider. The size already came from the stop.
wrong.Cancel the order and watch the close: The stop is a real order with the broker, not a watch of the close.
wrong.Widen it and sell shares to match: Selling shares does not make a lower stop OK. After the buy, the stop only moves up, never down or wider.

questions.story: You bought a spring at 52.40 with a real stop order at 51.10. The stock sags to 51.60 and you feel like dropping the stop to 50.20.
questions.simple: Leave the stop at 51.10, because after the buy a stop only moves up, never lower.

deeper.trap: Cutting shares to widen the stop feels like the same risk. It is not the plan. The size came from the honest stop at the buy, and after the entry the stop only moves up. A spring that fails usually fails at once, so the old stop is doing its job.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, D41)

questions.q: On a spring, the stop can move to breakeven at the first sell.
questions.why: True. We move the stop to breakeven between 2R and 5R, and the card sets it at the first sell by default. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R, but 3R sits inside that window.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, by default at the first sell.
questions.simple: True. By default the stop moves to breakeven at the first sell, and 3R is inside the window.

questions.q: Bought at 52.40 with the stop at 51.10. At what price is 2R, where the breakeven window opens?
questions.why: 55. One R is the buy minus the stop. 2R is the buy plus two of those, which is 55. Our breakeven window runs from 2R to 5R, and the card moves the stop to breakeven at the first trim by default. So 55 is where the window opens, not a point where you must move it.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 2R before the open. The breakeven window starts there.
questions.simple: 2R is 55, the buy plus twice the gap down to the stop.

questions.q: A spring position is 900 shares. You sell a third of the 900 at 3R and another third of the 900 at 5R. How many are left to trail?
questions.why: 300 shares. A third of 900 is 300. Two sells of 300 each leave the last 300, which you trail. Our rulebook calls these thirds adjustable.
questions.lesson_line: Two thirds sold, then trail the last third.
questions.simple: 300 shares are left, the last third, after selling a third in each of two sells.

questions.q: What does the plan do at 5R?
choices: Sell a third more; trail the rest
Sell everything and lock the gain in
Add a third back on the strength
Trail all of it under the 10-day
questions.answer: Sell a third more; trail the rest
questions.why: Sell a third more and trail the rest. In this plan, another third comes off at 5R after the first sell. The last third is trailed, under the 10-day for fast movers or the 21-day for steadier ones. Nothing is added, and the plan does not sell it all at once.
questions.lesson_line: After the first sell, a third at 5R, then trail the last third.

wrong.Sell everything and lock the gain in: The plan sells in thirds and trails the last one.
wrong.Add a third back on the strength: No adds. The full size is one price with one stop.
wrong.Trail all of it under the 10-day: The trail is only for the last third. A third comes off at 5R first.

questions.story: Your spring buy has made its first sell. Price now touches 5R and the stop is at breakeven.
questions.simple: Sell another third at 5R, then trail the last third, because this plan sells in thirds.

deeper.trap: The trap is to sell it all at 5R. The plan sells a third there and trails the last third under a rising average.

questions.q: Our card uses the Wyckoff price objective as the target rule for a spring.
questions.why: False. The card may show a Wyckoff target as a stop, look and listen level, not as a rule. ChartSchool says such targets are points to stop, look and listen, never exact turns. Our plan sells in parts and trails the rest, and the first sell is a judgment.
questions.lesson_line: A Wyckoff target is a place to look and listen. It is not a rule for the exit.
questions.simple: False. Our plan sells in parts and trails the rest, and a Wyckoff target is only a place to stop and look.

questions.q: In the Wyckoff school, how are price objectives measured?
choices: By twice the height of the range
By a fixed 3R on every trade
questions.why: By the point-and-figure count. ChartSchool says Wyckoff's cause can be measured by the horizontal point count in a Point and Figure chart. Pruden uses point and figure counts to calculate price projections. Our card notes that a target of twice the range height is in no source.
questions.lesson_line: Wyckoff objectives come from the point-and-figure count.

wrong.By twice the height of the range: No source behind this card uses that target.
wrong.By a fixed 3R on every trade: 3R is our own yardstick, not Wyckoff's objective. Our first sell is a judgment, not a fixed 3R.
wrong.By the prior all-time high: Wyckoff's objectives come from the count, not from a prior high.

questions.simple: By the point-and-figure count, because Wyckoff measures the cause built in a range with a horizontal count.

deeper.trap: A target of twice the range height looks like Wyckoff but is in no source, as our card notes. Even the real count is only a place to stop, look and listen.
